title: "Bias and Proxies"
---



## Rung 1 · Drop the Feature — And Watch It Fail

The naive fix writes itself: if the model must not depend on $S$, delete the
$S$ column.  It is also the fix every regulator first encounters, because it
*sounds* airtight — how can a model discriminate on information it never
receives?

Because other features **proxy** for it.  Zip code carries race; occupation
and hours-per-week carry sex; a sector dummy carries market beta.  The
mechanics are one line of regression algebra: the model fits

$$
\hat y = X\beta, \qquad\text{so}\qquad
\operatorname{Cov}(\hat y, S) = \beta^\top \operatorname{Cov}(X, S),
$$

and deleting the $S$ column only zeroes *one entry* of
$\operatorname{Cov}(X, S)$.  Every remaining feature that co-varies with $S$
keeps its channel open — and if $S$ genuinely predicts the target, the
optimizer will *actively recruit* those channels, because they carry signal
it is being paid to find.  Dropping the column does not remove the
dependence; it just reroutes it.

::: {#cell-fig-drop-fail .cell execution_count=2}
``` {.python .cell-code}
rng = np.random.default_rng(1)
n = 600
S = rng.normal(0, 1, n)                       # sensitive — to be "dropped"
proxy = S + 0.4 * rng.normal(0, 1, n)          # correlated feature — kept
x_legit = rng.normal(0, 1, n)                  # legitimate, S-independent
y = 0.7 * x_legit + 0.8 * S + 0.3 * rng.normal(0, 1, n)

# Train on [x_legit, proxy] only — S is NOT a feature.
X = np.column_stack([x_legit, proxy, np.ones(n)])
beta, *_ = np.linalg.lstsq(X, y, rcond=None)
y_hat = X @ beta
ck = cka_rbf(y_hat, S)

fig, (axL, axR) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(11, 4.2))

axL.scatter(proxy, S, s=12, c=WARM, alpha=0.5, edgecolors="none")
axL.set_title("The proxy still carries S", fontsize=12)
annotate_box(axL, 0.5, -0.10, f"corr(proxy, S) = {pearsonr(proxy, S)[0]:+.2f}")
axL.set_xlabel("kept feature (proxy)"); axL.set_ylabel("dropped S")
despine(axL)

axR.scatter(S, y_hat, s=12, c=COOL, alpha=0.5, edgecolors="none")
axR.set_title("So predictions still track S", fontsize=12)
annotate_box(axR, 0.5, -0.10, f"CKA(ŷ, S) = {ck:.2f}   (far from 0)")
axR.set_xlabel("dropped S"); axR.set_ylabel("prediction ŷ")
despine(axR)

fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display}
![We dropped S from the model, yet a kept proxy feature tracks it (left) — so the fitted predictions reconstruct the dependence anyway (right). The model never saw S; the optimizer found it regardless, because the proxy carried signal.](02-bias-and-proxies_files/figure-html/fig-drop-fail-output-1.png){#fig-drop-fail width=1304 height=489}
:::
:::


This is not a toy pathology.  In the
[real Census income data](../data/06-the-credit-dataset.qmd) the protected
attribute `sex` is dropped and the score reconstructs most of the income
gap anyway, riding chiefly on `occupation` — the
[credit lab](labs/lab-jobB-neutralize-credit.qmd) measures the leak
end-to-end.  And the leak is *distributed*: drop the worst proxy and the
others pick up the slack, which is why whacking proxies one at a time never
converges.

::: {.callout-tip}
## The Lesson in One Line
You cannot remove a dependence you refuse to look at.  Neutrality has to be
*measured against $S$* and optimized — which means $S$ must be available at
**training** time, even though it is never a model **input**.  That sounds
paradoxical until you see the
[three-layers picture](01-what-is-fair.qmd#the-three-layers): the audit
needs $S$ to test the dashed link; the model itself never touches it at
prediction time.
:::

## Algorithmic Bias — Balancing Errors *Within* Groups

"Don't use $S$" is not the only notion of fairness, and the failure above
shows why a second view matters: bias often shows up as **unequal error
rates across groups**.  A score can have the same average for two groups
yet be far more *wrong* for one of them — approving the uncreditworthy in
one group while declining the creditworthy in the other.  Criteria like
**equalized odds** target exactly this: independence of the *error*, not
the score, conditional on the true outcome.

::: {#cell-fig-group-errors .cell execution_count=3}
``` {.python .cell-code}
data = datasets.credit_scores_by_group(n=1500, gap=0.9, seed=0)
score, group, repaid = data["score"], data["group"], data["repaid"]
thr = 0.5

fig, (axL, axR) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(11, 4.0))

for g, col, name in [(0, COOL, "Group A"), (1, WARM, "Group B")]:
    axL.hist(score[group == g], bins=24, alpha=0.55, color=col, density=True,
             label=name)
axL.axvline(thr, color=INK, ls="--", lw=1.5, label="threshold")
axL.set_title("Score distribution by group", fontsize=12)
axL.set_xlabel("model score"); axL.set_ylabel("density")
axL.legend(fontsize=9, frameon=False)
despine(axL)

names, approval, fnr = [], [], []
for g, name in [(0, "Group A"), (1, "Group B")]:
    m = group == g
    approve = score[m] >= thr
    names.append(name)
    approval.append(approve.mean())
    # false-negative rate: creditworthy applicants wrongly declined
    good = repaid[m] == 1
    fnr.append((~approve[good]).mean() if good.any() else 0.0)

xpos = np.arange(len(names))
axR.bar(xpos - 0.18, approval, width=0.36, color=COOL, label="approval rate")
axR.bar(xpos + 0.18, fnr, width=0.36, color=CRASH,
        label="false-decline rate (creditworthy)")
axR.set_xticks(xpos); axR.set_xticklabels(names)
axR.set_title("Same threshold, different outcomes", fontsize=12)
axR.set_ylabel("rate")
axR.legend(fontsize=9, frameon=False)
despine(axR)

fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display}
![A scorecard with a group gap. Left: the score distributions sit at different heights, so one threshold cuts them differently. Right: the same threshold yields a lower approval rate AND a higher false-decline rate (creditworthy applicants wrongly refused) for Group B — the harm is concentrated, not averaged away.](02-bias-and-proxies_files/figure-html/fig-group-errors-output-1.png){#fig-group-errors width=1304 height=465}
:::
:::


The two views connect, and in the direction that matters for this chapter:
a prediction that is genuinely independent of $S$
($\operatorname{Dep}(\hat y, S) = 0$) cannot, by construction, carry a
systematic group gap in its scores.  Driving the dependence term to zero is
the **lever**; the group-rate table is how you **report** the result to the
people the model affects.  Keep both in view — the lab deliverables always
pair the dependence number with the per-group rates.

Next: the methods that actually remove the dependence —
[fair kernel learning](03-fair-kernel-learning.qmd).
